title: How Does a Cyclone Form, and Who Gives It a Name?
question: How does a tropical cyclone form, and who decides what it is called?
description: In early November 2026, a cyclone named Murasu formed in the Bay of Bengal and was forecast to reach India's south-east coast. The same kind of storm is called a hurricane or a typhoon elsewhere. In about five minutes, see how warm seawater becomes a spinning storm, why it turns the way it does, and how thirteen countries share one list of storm names. Every fact is checked against official weather agencies. Should storm names come from one shared international list, or should each country name the storms that hit it? Tell us in the comments.

ad_safety.reason: Educational weather explainer with no victim focus. Murasu and Arnab appear only as dated, factual examples, and the script gives no casualty details.

scenes.narration: In early November 2026, a storm over the Bay of Bengal became Cyclone Murasu, named on 1 November. As of 2 November, India's weather office expected landfall in Andhra Pradesh that night. How does a cyclone form?

visual.text: How does a cyclone form, and who names it?
visual.sub: Cyclone Murasu, Bay of Bengal, November 2026

scenes.narration: The same engine drives hurricanes in the Atlantic and typhoons in the Pacific. Today you will see how warm seawater becomes a spinning storm, and who decides what it is called.
In about five minutes, you will understand the ingredients, the spin, and the surprisingly international system of storm names.

visual.text: How does a calm sea become a storm?

scenes.narration: Scientists call them all tropical cyclones. They are called hurricanes in the Atlantic and eastern Pacific, typhoons in the western Pacific, and cyclones in the Indian Ocean.
Same physics, three words. Which one you use depends on which part of the world the storm is born in.
The North Indian Ocean is the least active official basin, producing only about six to seven percent of the world's tropical cyclones. Yet it has its own busy seasons.

visual.label: of the world's tropical cyclones form here

scenes.narration: Storms there tend to form between April and June, and again between October and December, so a cyclone in early November is not out of season.
Everything starts with warm water. The sea needs to be at least twenty-six and a half degrees Celsius, and that warmth must reach about fifty metres down.
Warm water evaporates, and the moist air rises. High up it cools, the vapour condenses into cloud, and that condensation releases heat.
That released heat keeps the air rising. In effect, the storm is a heat engine, running on the gap between the warm sea and the cold air far above.
As air rises, pressure at the surface falls, and surrounding air rushes in. That new air warms, gathers moisture and rises too, so the loop feeds itself.
A heap of rising air is not yet a spinning storm. So why does a cyclone rotate?
The answer is the spin of the Earth. Moving air is deflected sideways: to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern.
So low pressure spins counterclockwise north of the equator and clockwise south of it. A storm over the Bay of Bengal turns counterclockwise; one off Madagascar turns clockwise.
Near the equator this effect is too weak, so tropical cyclones rarely form within about five degrees of latitude of it. Most form roughly between 5 and 20 degrees from the equator.

visual.label: latitude: storms rarely form closer to the equator

scenes.narration: So the recipe has four parts: warm water, thunderstorms, a little spin from the Earth, and winds that do not change much with height.
That last part matters. Strong winds high up can rip a storm's structure apart, and even when every ingredient is present, a storm does not always develop.

visual.label: Wind shear
visual.sub: strong upper winds tear storms apart

scenes.narration: As a storm strengthens, an opening forms at its centre, called the eye. It is ringed by the eyewall, where much of the storm's heat is released.
Satellite images of Murasu in early November 2026 showed clear spiral bands of cloud, the visible sign of a storm that had organised itself.

India's weather office grades storms in steps. Murasu began as a low-pressure area, became a deep depression on 1 November, a named cyclonic storm that day, and severe on 2 November. Higher grades: very severe, extremely severe, super cyclonic.

As of 2 November, India's weather office forecast landfall winds of 100 to 110 kilometres an hour, gusting to 120. That was weaker than Cyclone Arnab in late October 2026, which hit with about 125 to 135 kilometres an hour.

visual.label: forecast on 2 November: landfall winds, gusts to 120

scenes.narration: A storm keeps strengthening only while it has warm water to feed on. Over cooler water, evaporation falls and the storm weakens.
Now to the names. Naming began so storms could be identified quickly in warnings, because names are far easier to remember than numbers and technical terms.
Atlantic storms have been named from lists since 1953. The North Indian Ocean began naming in 2004, and a new list of names was adopted in 2020.
In the North Indian Ocean, thirteen countries, from Bangladesh to Yemen, each contributed names to one shared list. Murasu, the storm of November 2026, carries India's contribution.
Names are taken in order. When a storm reaches roughly sixty-two kilometres an hour, the regional weather centre in New Delhi gives it the next name on the list.
That list holds one hundred and sixty-nine names, thirteen from each member country, and names in this region are not repeated.

visual.label: names on the Indian Ocean list

scenes.narration: Crucially, the name is not chosen afresh by the country the storm hits. It simply comes next from the approved list.

visual.label: Pre-approved list
visual.sub: not picked by the country hit

scenes.narration: Elsewhere, a storm that is especially deadly or costly can have its name retired for good. In the Atlantic, one hundred names have been retired as of 2026.
Atlantic lists repeat every six years unless a name is retired. Until 1979 they held only women's names, and since then they have mixed men's and women's names.
In one breath: warm seawater feeds rising, moist air, the Earth's rotation spins it into a storm, and a shared list of names helps warnings travel fast.
Here is a question for you. Should storm names come from one shared international list, as now, or should each country name the storms that strike it? Tell us in the comments.
